title: KR Releases 14th Issue of Decarbonization Magazine, Covering Marine Small Modular Reactors and First-Year FuelEU Maritime Compliance Trends
summary: The first year of FuelEU Maritime reveals a critical regulatory failure, as 92% of ships avoided penalties through compliance pooling. This widespread credit trading caused compliance surpluses to plummet 80% below the penalty level, proving the current framework offers no real incentive for actual carbon intensity reduction. While discussions on complex marine SMRs and methane slip abatement continue, immediate emissions accountability remains elusive.
content:
An examination of emerging regulatory frameworks for marine small modular reactors (SMRs), including challenges associated with their application onboard ships and safety approval.

An analysis of the first year of FuelEU Maritime, highlighting compliance trends and their implications for decarbonization strategies

Korean Register (KR) released the 14th issue of its quarterly KR Decarbonization Magazine on October 29. The latest issue covers emerging marine SMR regulation, the first-year results of FuelEU Maritime, and technologies to cut methane slip from LNG-fueled engines.

The issue opens with an examination of the regulatory frameworks for marine SMRs and the challenges of installing reactors on vessels, including safety assurance, maintenance requirements, and the cost and complexity of obtaining approvals. The article also reviews recent IMO revision work, the IMO–IAEA collaboration and KR’s own technical projects.

While the regulatory framework for marine SMRs is still under development, FuelEU Maritime, by contrast, is already in effect, and the magazine analyzes its first year of compliance. Ships that fail to meet the mandatory greenhouse gas intensity limits can avoid penalties by pooling their compliance balances with over-compliant vessels. According to KR’s analysis, approximately 92% of ships used pooling in the first year, while the price of compliance surpluses gradually declined to approximately 80% below the penalty level.

Turning from regulation to technology, the issue also features an interview with Minho Kang, Senior Vice President at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, on engine optimization and exhaust aftertreatment technologies. He discusses the company’s Methane Oxidation Catalyst System (MOCS), which oxidizes unburned methane escaping from LNG-fueled engines.
